terms.gloss: imperative; as a noun (modus understood), the imperative
evidence: Mart. Cap. 3.313 and the grammarians (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: modus imperātīvus, the imperative mood: lege!, legite! (Traupman 229). To form the imperative of a verb is facere imperātīvum (Traupman 246). We have found no classical name for it; Quintilian contrasts nē and nōn as vetandī and negandī, of forbidding and of denying (1.5.50).

phrases.latin: Dīc imperātīvum modum ejusdem verbī, tempore praesentī, singulāriter et plūrāliter.
phrases.english: Give the present imperative of the same verb in the singular and the plural.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 225, p. 229, p. 246, p. 247.
Quintilian checked against the Perseus Latin texts, and cited by its numbering.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
